data.title: Berlin's run-down public spaces at heart of election campaign
data.description:
Berlin's run-down public spaces at heart of election campaign

Pierrick YVON
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 5:23 am UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Politicians campaigning for Sunday's Berlin state election have painted an unflattering picture of the German capital, vowing to clear garbage-strewn streets and promising "syringe-free playgrounds".

Town hall-hopefuls have also pledged to clean up graffiti-covered train stations, end "forever-building sites", fix buckled cycling lanes and take steps to ease a desperate shortage of affordable housing.

Taken together, the list of woes hardens the image of a chronically broke city whose administration often struggles to reliably provide services for its almost four million people.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Certainly, many who live in Berlin love its rich artistic and cultural life, green spaces, lakes and children's playgrounds, vibrant start-up scene and hedonistic, anything-goes nightlife.

The long-divided city boasts countless museums, galleries and sites reflecting its troubled history, as well as two zoos, three opera houses and multiple techno clubs known around the world.

But all of that has gone hand-in-hand with persistent complaints about a slow bureaucracy and a dysfunctional city administration which famously took almost 15 years to build an international airport with next-door Brandenburg state.

Cross-financed by Germany's wealthier states, Berlin is deep in the red, with 2.2 billion euros in debt calculated in late 2024, which forced painful spending cuts in multiple areas.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Berlin's former mayor Klaus Wowereit once famously labelled Berlin "poor but sexy" -- but since then many of its residents have at times struggled to stay in love with the city.

- 'Garbage mountains' -

Local newspapers often write about Berlin's "crime hotspots" and rising homelessness, and make great sport of documenting ever-new Berlin disasters -- from rat-infested police stations to the closure of the Technical University's main campus due to structural defects and fire safety issues.

With renovations now set to cost around 2.4 billion euros, university president Fatma Deniz blamed "decades of delayed investment and budget cuts in public infrastructure".

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The small party Volt has been running campaign posters with the promise to "unf*ck berlin" that list a litany of complaints from potholes to "garbage mountains" and, more generally, "Berlin frustration".

One Berlin resident fed up with filthy streets has taken matters into her own hands.

Valeriia Tantcyreva, 31, started the volunteer group Sauberberlin (Clean Berlin), which on a recent outing in the working-class district of Wedding filled a secure disposal box with syringes discarded by drug users.

"No one cares about the city," she charged, calling the waste management service "useless". She said she decided to take action after her dog was repeatedly injured by broken glass and other refuse.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

City hall told AFP, when asked about the garbage problem, that there were "no operational failures", pointing instead to many residents' lack of civic responsibility.

Another pet peeve for many are sketchy cycling lanes in a city where 18 percent of all trips are made by bike.

They are often "outdated, too narrow, overgrown with vegetation and buckled by tree roots", complained Lisa Feitsch of the cycling association ADFC.

- 'Chaos city' -

The city's politics may be even messier than its streets, and the next government is certain to again be run by a multi-party coalition.

Four parties are leading the race for the Rotes Rathaus (Red Town Hall), all polling in the range of 16 to 21 percent, with the centre-left SPD trailing behind them.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Frontrunners for the top spot are the centre-right CDU -- which is strongest in Berlin's leafy western suburbs -- and the far-left Die Linke, whose heartland lies in parts of the former east.

The far-right AfD, whose bastion is among the communist-era residential tower blocks of the former East Berlin, expects new record results -- but also to remain shut out of power by all other parties.

Also among the top four are the Greens, who dominate in hip inner-city areas known for trendy cafes, organic supermarkets and cargo bicycles.

When Berlin voters head to the polls on Sunday, they will hope to elect a capable new government -- but also simply that the city-state doesn't mess up the vote itself, like it did in 2021.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Citizens back then waited in hours-long queues while some polling booths ran out of ballot papers and resupplies were obstructed by a marathon the city had decided to stage on the same day.

The 2021 election fiasco, as well as subsequent street unrest on New Year's Eve, led the Bavarian state premier Markus Soeder, based in far tidier Munich, to thunder that Berlin was a "chaos city".

Berlin eventually held a successful re-run of the vote in 2023.

data.title: SpaceX's first Starfall customer is European mission integrator Space Cargo
data.description:
By Joey Roulette

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - SpaceX's new Starfall business of returning products and other payloads from Earth's orbit has signed a mission deal with integrator Space Cargo as the unit's first customer, the company's Chief Executive Nicolas Gaume told Reuters.

Space Cargo aims to fly in ‌2028 an orbital reentry flight on the first commercial mission of Starship, which will deploy SpaceX's Starfall - a disk-shaped capsule designed to carry materials ‌on short trips through orbit and back to Earth.

Launched aboard Falcon 9 and eventually Starship, Starfall is an aluminum housing protected by a 10-foot (3-m) -wide heatshield that SpaceX offers to customers seeking to make ​products or do research in the microgravity of space.

Luxembourg-based Space Cargo will place its "BentoBox" system in the Starfall capsule, positioning itself as an integrator in the SpaceX program with plans to book more such future missions, Space Cargo CEO Gaume said.

"We're flying 200 kilos with our current systems, but with Starship and Starfall, we're going to go to ton and tons" of customer payloads, "and that's really what we want," he added.

The box would secure up to 1 ton of different types of payloads from Space Cargo's own ‌customers that it signed up for the mission, allowing them ⁠to survive reentry and be safely returned to Earth for commercial use.

The Space Cargo deal is the first known customer for SpaceX's Starfall program, which emerged quickly earlier this year before demonstrating a capsule mission in June.

The product's central capability is its ⁠heatshield, a commodification of SpaceX's experience ferrying its larger Dragon capsules between Earth and space mainly for NASA.

The first BentoBox on a Starfall capsule will be among payloads on SpaceX's first commercial mission with Starship, SpaceX's giant next-generation rocket under development, Gaume said.

That mission is planned for 2028, Space Cargo said in a statement.

SpaceX, which did not respond to a request ​for ​comment, has not previously said when Starship will fly its first commercial mission.

The emerging business ​of returning payloads from space is valuable for customers such as ‌drugmakers relying on the microgravity of space for research and production involving higher purities impossible to attain in Earth's gravity.

There are unique benefits of in-space production of other products, such as fiber optic cables, which are of higher quality when produced in microgravity on the International Space Station, NASA has said.

Nearly half Space Cargo's potential customers for its first Starfall mission are in the life sciences and biotechnology sectors, the company said.

The Starfall program joins a growing industry of capsule reentry services, where SpaceX faces rivalry from smaller startups such as California-based Varda Space, whose flagship capsule has flown 6 missions and lands in an Australian desert.

The Pentagon has seen ‌capsule reentry missions, which must aerodynamically steer through the blazing-hot hypersonic speeds of atmospheric reentry, as ​useful for research and tests involving hypersonic weapons and as potential target practice for its Golden ​Dome missile defense program.

Gaume said flying its BentoBox with Starship and Starfall ​promises a fast pace of missions as SpaceX targets an unprecedented Starship flight rate once the rocket emerges from development.

BentoBox has plans ‌to fly with other capsules, such as German startup ATMOS ​Space Cargo's Phoenix craft and the European Space ​Agency's Space Rider.

"It's really the volume and the rhythm" that makes the Starfall deal key, added Gaume, who declined to detail pricing and costs.

Starship is nearing routine flights but its development has been years behind schedule.

Its next text flight sometime this year, the 14th since 2023, will seek to put ​its first SpaceX-built Starlink satellites in orbit, followed by ‌increasingly frequent in-house satellite launches that have come to dominate SpaceX's schedule.

The 2028 target for Starship's first commercial mission suggests several of the ​rocket's first flights throughout 2027 will serve SpaceX's Starlink satellite unit, and possibly its Starmind business of putting AI data centers in space ​if those satellites are ready in time.

(Reporting by Joey Roulette; Editing by Clarence Fernandez)

data.title: Gates Foundation to spend $1.27 billion to expand AI access to poor, remote communities
data.description:
Gates Foundation to spend $1.27 billion to expand AI access to poor, remote communities

Audrey Tan
Updated Tue, 15 September 2026 at 4:15 am UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

SINGAPORE – The Gates Foundation, a philanthropic organisation backed by US billionaire Bill Gates, pledged on Sept 15 to spend at least US$1 billion (S$1.27 billion) globally over the next two years on expanding access to artificial intelligence.

With the foundation having opened its Singapore office in May, chief executive Mark Suzman told The Straits Times that it is looking into how more people in the region, especially those from lower-income and rural areas, could benefit from using AI in areas such as education, agriculture and health.

He cited the Asia Pathogen Genomics Initiative – established at the Duke-NUS Centre for Outbreak Preparedness in late 2021 with the goal of eliminating infectious diseases – as an example of past work in the health-AI nexus that the foundation had supported.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Now operating in 15 countries across the region, the initiative has an AI-enabled bioinformatics program called PathGen, Suzman said. The program helps detect emerging disease threats earlier, assess risks faster, and coordinate responses within and across borders.

Such projects offer a glimpse of what the foundation could support, Suzman said, adding that "the commitment is across education, agriculture, and health."

He was speaking to The Straits Times in a video interview on Sept 11, ahead of the launch of the foundation's latest Goalkeepers report on Sept 15. The annual report takes stock of the world's progress on issues such as ending poverty and reducing inequalities.

The latest edition highlights the need to ensure that AI is used to narrow gaps between the richest and poorest, not widen them.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The Gates Foundation was created in part to address a basic market failure: The people with the greatest needs often have the least power to shape where innovation and investment go," Bill Gates, chairman of the foundation, noted in the report.

"AI presents the same challenge, only at much greater speed. Left to the market alone, the most capable tools will be built first for the people and institutions most able to pay for them – not necessarily for those who could benefit most."

Of the US$1 billion sum, 40 per cent will go to education, such as AI tutoring initiatives, said the Gates Foundation in a statement.

Another 40 per cent will go towards healthcare, which could include the development of tools that can help in the discovery of new drugs and vaccines. A further 10 per cent will be for agriculture, supporting efforts to give smallholder farmers AI-generated advice customised to their soil, weather and crop conditions, for instance.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The remaining 10 per cent will fund initiatives to help build the digital foundation needed for equitable AI access. This could include ensuring that datasets in languages not yet understood by AI tools are incorporated.

The report cited MahaVISTAAR, a free AI advisory service for farmers rolled out by the Indian state of Maharashtra, as an example of an AI tool that can benefit smallholder farmers.

Through an app, voice calls and chat, farmers can ask questions about their crops, the weather, and pest management in their own language and get verified, localised answers, the report noted. The service costs the government less than 18 US cents per farmer.

Suzman said: "We need to make sure that AI is able to work in every spoken language, with a particular focus on languages in Asia and Africa, and so we are working with a range of partners to see how we can help facilitate that."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

This could include working with the private sector and governments, he said.

"There are significant philanthropic resources in Singapore, Malaysia generally, which we would be able to capitalise on," he added.

On the importance of training AI models in other languages, the report pointed to an example from Malawi.

"A woman in labour might say her 'water has broken' in Chichewa. Translated directly to English, it would sound like she has simply 'thrown away water'. That mistranslation could be the difference between timely, urgent medical advice and tragedy," noted the 72-page report.

AI tools also need to be grounded in local data, the report said. For instance, a community health worker in Rwanda examining a baby with a fever faces different questions from a clinician in a well-resourced hospital.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The AI supporting her needs to reflect that," the report said.

It also highlighted the importance of ensuring that communities themselves are trained to use AI, and have the right access to these tools.

This would require a mix of approaches, the foundation noted in the report. These include price reductions, commitments from AI companies to make their models and computing resources available, and government and philanthropic funding.

The foundation said its committed funding will support partners already working to close the gaps in access to AI and ensure that AI tools reflect the knowledge and priorities of the people who need them most.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"We can harness AI for good. But it won't happen by accident," Gates said in the report.

"It requires a deliberate, specific commitment from government leaders and the companies developing the technology: to measure success not only by what AI can do for the most profitable users but by what it can do for the people who stand the most to gain."

Correction note: The Gates Foundation has clarified that it opened its Singapore office in May.

Source: The Straits Times © SPH Media Limited. Permission required for reproduction

data.title: A Sacramento woman was fatally shot by a longtime stalker. DHS says he was in the country illegally
data.description:
A Sacramento woman was fatally shot by a longtime stalker. DHS says he was in the country illegally

Alisha Ebrahimji, CNN
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 4:07 am UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

A California woman was fatally shot in Sacramento last week by a man authorities said had been stalking her for months and the Department of Homeland Security said had been living in the country illegally.

Deputies with the Sacramento County Sheriff's Office responded to a scene near a restaurant just before 3 p.m. on September 8, after several witnesses reported a shooting, the agency said in a news release.

Authorities have not publicly identified the 38-year-old victim, but CNN affiliate KCRA spoke with her mother and reported her to be Sacramento resident Shalini Thakur.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Police identified the suspect as Rohit Rohit, 22, an Indian man who entered the United States through Arizona in 2023, the DHS told CNN Monday.

Thakur's grieving mother, Sudesh Kumari, who said goodbye to her only child at her funeral Monday, is left wondering if more could have been done to protect her daughter, she told KCRA.

Kumari and Thakur's uncle were the only family present at the funeral, with the rest of her family in India, CNN affiliate KMAX/KOVR reported. Everyone else in attendance was a friend –– even a customer of the IHOP she worked at.

"I want to honor her heart and her kindness," Melinda Willey, who later became friends with Thakur, told KMAX/KOVR.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"She was a lady with a vibrant personality. Larger than life, with this glow about her, her aura," Satinder Dulai, a friend of Thakur's told the outlet. "She had a bubbly personality. She had a lot of goals. And I think one by one, she was completing them. She was a little feisty, but very loving."

Suspect met victim picking up DoorDash orders

Rohit and Thakur knew each other through work. Thakur said she met Rohit when he picked up DoorDash orders from the business where she worked, according to court documents obtained by KCRA.

Rohit signed up to work for the delivery company using a Social Security number and completed a background check through an accredited provider, a DoorDash spokesperson told CNN Monday. Rohit had not worked in more than six weeks, according to the spokesperson, was not active on the app the day of the shooting, and the company never received any prior reports about him.

"This is an unimaginable tragedy, and our hearts are with Ms. Thakur's family and loved ones as they grieve this immense loss," a DoorDash spokesperson said.

Authorities said they are still investigating the immediate events that led up to the fatal shooting but have learned Rohit was waiting for Thakur at a local shopping center, where she was dropped off at her own vehicle a short time after. It's unclear who dropped her off or where she was coming from.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Rohit approached Thakur "and began to accost her," the Sacramento County Sheriff's Office said in the news release, adding, "As the victim attempted to run away, Rohit chased her down, pulled out a firearm, and shot her multiple times." Thakur fell to the ground and Rohit fired additional shots, the sheriff's office said.

Sacramento County Sheriff Jim Cooper released a brief, blurry video on Facebook, which he said showed Rohit shooting Thakur.

Witnesses told authorities the suspect fled the area but gave a description of his car to guide deputies as they worked to locate him.

Investigators used Flock, an automated license-plate reader system at the center of a national debate over privacy, to track down the suspect's vehicle and within minutes, the deputies located the car. As they tried to pull it over, the driver slammed on the brakes, and after attempting to call the driver out of the car, deputies discovered Rohit died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Homeland Security highlights suspect's immigration status

"This tragedy would have been completely avoided if it weren't for the Biden Administration RELEASING this killer into our country," a DHS spokesperson told CNN in a statement Monday. "Sanctuary politicians must put an end to reckless policies that play Russian roulette with American lives. Our thoughts and prayers are with the victim and her family."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

California Gov. Gavin Newsom pushed back on DHS' response to the incident, which the department said stemmed from California's sanctuary state law, the California Values Act, which prohibits local law enforcement from using its resources for immigration enforcement, with limited exceptions.

"Trying to turn a horrific act of stalking and domestic violence into an indictment of California's sanctuary policies is not supported by the evidence and distracts from the real issues this case raises — law enforcement preventing stalking and domestic violence, enforcing restraining orders, and keeping victims safe," Newsom's spokesperson Diana Crofts-Pelayo told CNN.

While the incident has drawn attention to the suspect's immigration status, a National Institute of Justice summary of a Texas-based study found undocumented immigrants were arrested at less than half the rate of native-born US citizens for violent and drug-related crimes. Immigrants are also incarcerated at lower rates, according to the National Bureau of Economic Research.

Apple AirTag under car's hood and punctured tires

Rohit's alleged stalking and harassment started in at least January when Thakur found an Apple AirTag under the hood of her car, according to investigators, and grew over the months as efforts intensified in nature and severity.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The suspect's actions "had grown increasingly alarming" during one incident when he deflated the air in Thakur's car tires and followed her to her workplace so he could help her, the Sacramento County Sheriff's Office said.

Separately, in another incident, Rohit obtained a copy of Thakur's apartment key, entered while she was sleeping and then claimed he was there because he was worried something happened to her when she didn't answer him, the sheriff's office said.

"Despite the bizarre behavior, the victim initially declined to pursue charges or obtain a restraining order," the sheriff's office said. "Deputies and Detectives remained concerned for her safety and remained in contact with the victim for the next few months."

In May, Thakur obtained a restraining order against Rohit after deputies urged her to do so again, authorities said. In late July, authorities said he violated the order when he dropped groceries off at her door.

Four months later, she was dead

How the situation escalated from deliveries to a shooting in a parking lot remains a mystery. The sheriff's office said its investigation is ongoing, as the case draws national attention and political barbs.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Thakur's loved ones are honoring her life online with written memories from former co-workers and newfound friends on an obituary page for her.

On a GoFundMe page raising money to support Thakur's family, an organizer described her as "a caring, loving, selfless, and generous young woman who gave so much of herself to others" and someone whose kindness and willingness to help others has left a lasting impact on everyone who knew her.

National Domestic Violence Hotline: Call 1-800-799-SAFE (7233), or text "START" to 88788, which connects callers with local resources and immediate support. Help is also available through an online chat tool.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

data.title: South Korea to develop new security guidelines for autonomous AI agents
data.description:
South Korea to develop new security guidelines for autonomous AI agents

Reuters
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 4:24 am UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

SEOUL, Sept 15 (Reuters) - South Korea's state-run internet security agency said on Tuesday it is developing ‌updated guidelines to manage the growing autonomy of ‌AI systems, as companies deploy AI agents capable of operating with ​limited human oversight.

Here are the details:

• The Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA), which operates under South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT, told Reuters it is working on an updated ‌version of the "AI ⁠Security Guide", first published last year.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

• In a statement, KISA said the revised guide would ⁠focus on security issues that could arise as companies deploy agentic AI services and offer a checklist to manage ​those ​risks.

• The agency also said ​the guide could include ‌common control measures applicable to "physical AI" systems capable of interacting with real-world devices and machinery.

• KISA said the new guide was designed to address risks posed by agentic AI systems more broadly and not specifically targeted at ‌high-performance AI models, such as ​those implicated in the Hugging Face ​breach.

• The July ​hack of the open-source repository Hugging Face, ‌in which a swarm of ​roughly 700 AI ​agents created by OpenAI carried out a hack and in many cases tried to cover their ​tracks, has become ‌a catalyst for a broader industry reckoning over ​how to govern increasingly autonomous AI systems.

(Reporting by ​Joyce LeeEditing by Ed Davies)

data.title: Justices Alito, Thomas Dismiss Impacts Of Trump’s Mail Voting Overhaul Attempt In Dissent
data.description:
Justices Alito, Thomas Dismiss Impacts Of Trump’s Mail Voting Overhaul Attempt In Dissent

Taiyler S. Mitchell
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 4:08 am UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

Justice Samuel Alito dismissed the potential consequences of President Donald Trump's last-minute attempt to overhaul mail voting ahead of the November midterms in his dissent to the Supreme Court's Monday night ruling.

Trump's March executive order called on the U.S. Postal Service to implement new rules for mail ballots, including individualized barcodes printed on all mail ballots and the submission of lists of mail voters to the federal government ahead of time. But some states have already mailed ballots to voters for the midterms.

Politics: 'Hoax': FCC Chair Rips Kimmel-Talarico Interview As Clip Takes Off On YouTube

A coalition of Democrat-led states sued to stop the effort because of the possibilities of widespread confusion and delays, as well as voters being "denied the ability to vote." Opponents were also concerned about the potential cost to implement the order.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"No election office, at any level of government, has budgeted for the work the Rule requires," a brief in the case from current and former GOP election officials stated. 

On Monday night, the Supreme Court declined to lift a preliminary injunction blocking the implementation of Trump's order.

"In my view, based on the briefing the Court has received at this interim stage, there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority," Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in a brief concurrence. "But applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections."

Politics: McConnell Returns To The Senate For The First Time Since June

In his dissent, which was joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, Alito said it was important for the government to be able to "better detect election fraud."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

While Alito was concerned that the rule would be very difficult to implement so close to the election, he concluded that it was "not enough to convince me."

Alito also blamed the states and the courts for the timing and argued that the USPS retains "broad authority to regulate the mail."

Voter fraud is a rare issue that Trump and his allies relentlessly continue to claim, particularly with regard to the 2020 election that he lost to former President Joe Biden. However, he has not claimed any of the other elections Republicans won were "stolen."

Politics: Joe Scarborough Praises 1 Democrat That Republicans 'Really Don't Know What To Do With'

The midterm elections are scheduled for Nov. 3.

data.title: Wiping out measles impossible due to vaccine hesitancy in rich countries, says Gates
data.description:
Wiping out measles impossible due to vaccine hesitancy in rich countries, says Gates

By Jennifer Rigby
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 4:08 am UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Jennifer Rigby

LONDON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Vaccine hesitancy in rich countries means ending measles as a global public health threat is not currently possible, Bill Gates told Reuters in an interview.

The ‌Microsoft co-founder turned billionaire philanthropist said wiping out the killer childhood disease had previously been a ‌potential goal for his eponymous foundation, which focuses on global health and the world's poorest people.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But it was now off the table ​due to increased vaccine hesitancy in wealthier nations, part of a wave of skepticism championed for decades by the now health secretary in the United States under President Donald Trump, Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

"At one point, the foundation wanted to eradicate measles, but the vaccine hesitancy in rich countries has meant that's not on our list of goals," Gates ‌said. "I think that's kind of tragic."

MEASLES ⁠RISE

Measles, among the world's most contagious diseases, causes a high fever, a cough and a tell-tale rash.

The virus killed around 2 million children every year before the introduction of ⁠a vaccine in the 1960s. Nowadays, around 100,000 children die annually, largely in countries where conflict or logistics make immunisation difficult. The WHO says vaccination rates need to be above 95% to prevent outbreaks.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But recent years have also seen a ​surge ​in cases in countries where the disease was almost forgotten, ​including in the United States and Europe, ‌as vaccination rates have fallen.

Gates said that vaccine hesitancy had at least not spread to lower-income countries, where measles can be much deadlier than in richer countries due to malnutrition and healthcare gaps.

"There's always that concern that if you have doubters in the U.S., that becomes a global thing," he said. "But we haven't seen an increase in vaccine hesitancy in the countries the foundation works in."

AID CUTS

Gates was speaking ahead of the foundation's annual ‌Goalkeepers event, which looks at progress towards the United Nations ​global development goals set for 2030, including on improving health.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In last ​year's report, Gates warned of the impact of ​aid cuts led by Trump's administration, and followed by other wealthy countries like the ‌UK and Germany, on the health of the ​world's poorest.

This year, he said ​the cuts had likely caused many deaths, but the restoration of some money had prevented the worst-case scenario. Efforts from impacted countries and other health groups also held off disaster, as Reuters has reported.

"The ​most dire predictions, which went above ‌10 million deaths, we don't see that taking place," Gates said, adding that he continued ​to urge governments to restore aid or at least not cut it further. "It's still a very ​tragic situation."

(Reporting by Jennifer Rigby; Editing by Hugh Lawson)

data.title: Saudi Arabia warns it will react 'firmly' to Houthi attacks
data.description:
Saudi Arabia warns it will react 'firmly' to Houthi attacks

AFP News
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 4:07 am UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Saudi Arabia warned Tuesday it will react "firmly" to Yemen's Houthis, after a series of attacks carried out by the pro-Iranian rebels using ballistic missiles and drones wounded 13 civilians in the country's south.

The Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with Saudi-backed government forces since Yemen's civil war reignited in July, when the group declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh and began targeting its ships in the Red Sea.

The group seized control of Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait last week, which has become vital as the wider US-Iran war chokes the Strait of Hormuz, in a significant blow to Yemeni government forces.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

It has also targeted the oil infrastructure of Saudi Arabia, the world's leading crude exporter, pushing oil prices above the $100 threshold.

A Houthi strike in western Yemen on Monday killed eight soldiers from government forces, according to two military sources.

The Houthis claimed a new "large-scale" attack using "dozens of ballistic missiles and drones" against the King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, in southern Saudi Arabia.

A Khamis Mushait resident told AFP he heard "intense blasts" which left fires burning for a "long time".

"Honestly, we couldn't sleep at all."

The Riyadh-led coalition confirmed Tuesday there had been missile and drone attacks the previous day on Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif, reporting 13 wounded.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Riyadh responded with more than 50 strikes, as it had the day before, according to the Houthis.

The coalition said it would deal with the attacks "firmly to protect the sovereignty of the Kingdom" and would take "all necessary operational measures to deter this... hostile and extremist approach".

Hazem al-Assad from the Houthis' politburo said the "Yemeni response will continue and escalate as long as they (Saudi Arabia) persist in their aggression against our people".

In the early hours of Tuesday, Saudi civil defence issued air-raid alerts in six regions, before lifting them.

The renewed fighting in Yemen comes as the wider regional war remains at a stalemate. But US President Donald Trump on Monday said he was open to holding talks with Iran.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The failing Nation of Iran wants to make a deal, quickly and badly. I will determine whether or not the U.S.A. will choose to engage -- The concept of which we are open to," Trump said on his Truth Social network.

Iran's top security chief Mohsen Rezaei said on X that "there will be no negotiations until Iran's conditions are met. That is all there is to it".

- Wider regional war -

A proposed meeting between Gulf states and Iran over the future of Hormuz was postponed on Monday, with Tehran accusing Riyadh of using Yemen as a "pretext" to delay the talks.

Tehran has long supported the Houthis, a member of its anti-Israel "axis of resistance", including with weapons and technology, but analysts dispute the extent to which Iran is behind the renewed fighting.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Iran does not interfere in Yemeni affairs," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told reporters on Monday, saying the Houthis are "entirely independent actors who make their decisions based on their own interests".

Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was expected to hold talks with Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Tuesday, Cairo announced.

US media reported last week Trump had rejected a personal request from the Saudi crown prince to intervene in the war.

- Forced to flee -

Yemeni government forces on Sunday said they had recaptured positions in the southwestern province of Taiz from Houthi fighters and carried out airstrikes, telling the official Saba news agency they killed at least 10 gunmen.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Saudi crown prince received US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper in Jeddah on Monday to discuss "the latest developments in the region", according to Saudi news agency SPA.

The admiral travelled to Saudi Arabia on Thursday for urgent coordination meetings, according to US news site Axios.

The Houthis seized Yemen's capital Sanaa in 2014 at the outset of the civil war, driving the government to Aden in the south.

The following year, Saudi Arabia led a coalition to intervene on the side of the government, launching wave after wave of airstrikes as the conflict escalated into one of the worst humanitarian disasters in the world.

The UN's migration agency said Monday the renewed fighting in the Arab world's poorest country had forced 93,864 people to flee their homes.

data.title: Governments worldwide are way behind on AI, says Bill Gates
data.description:
Governments worldwide are way behind on AI, says Bill Gates

By Jennifer Rigby
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 4:06 am UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Jennifer Rigby

LONDON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - No government in the world is ready for the changes artificial intelligence will bring to society, Bill Gates said in an interview with Reuters, as he warned of ‌the risks ahead.

The Microsoft co-founder and billionaire philanthropist had until recently been optimistic about AI, but has changed his ‌position, warning of the threats to jobs, concerns about attacks and the dangers of addiction to AI companions.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I don't think any government is nearly as ​deep on this as they have to be," he said. However, he added that the technology has great potential to help the world's poorest if managed properly and accessed equally — and his namesake foundation said on Tuesday that it plans to spend at least $1 billion in the next two years on expanding access to AI.

Gates said he has been talking to world leaders ‌about his concerns, including President Donald Trump ⁠and his team in the U.S., and said he aims to meet China's President Xi Jinping later this year.

"Governments are way behind on this one," he added.

HEALTH POTENTIAL

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But despite his concerns, Gates and his ⁠foundation hope AI can help narrow gaps between the richest and poorest, rather than widening them.

The foundation's $1 billion spending plan, part of its previously announced plans to spend $9 billion annually, will go to partners working in education, healthcare and agriculture, the foundation said. It ​also ​aims to help build the data foundations AI is built on, ​such as ensuring that large language models work ‌in every language people speak.

"For health it's hard to overstate what the potential is," Gates said, from supporting frontline health care workers to discovering new drugs and vaccines.

But he said governments must work together to avoid problems, likening the arrival of AI to a disaster movie.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"There's all sorts of movies where some aliens are coming, and magically the U.S. and China and everybody comes together to solve the problem," he said. "AI is kind of like this alien intelligence. It's here, and we better ‌do like it shows in those movies."

REPUTATIONAL HIT?

In June, Gates appeared ​in front of Congress to testify about his relationship with the late ​convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Gates, who is not ​accused of any crimes, has repeatedly said he regrets his association with Epstein, who he hoped ‌would donate to global health causes. Instead, the ​financier attempted to blackmail Gates over ​his extramarital affairs.

However, despite prompting an external review at his foundation, which found no payments to Epstein or participation in criminal activities, Gates said the links had not caused him or the foundation a significant reputational hit.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"In terms ​of having access to government leaders, or ‌you know, journalists being willing to interview me, I don't see any diminishment," he said, adding that the ​desire to draw on the foundation's expertise to cut child deaths and end malaria had also not ​reduced "even one iota".

(Reporting by Jennifer Rigby; Editing by Hugh Lawson)

Russia hits petrol station, warehouse facilities in Kyiv, mayor says

Reuters
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 3:35 am UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Russian drone strike in Kyiv

1 of 3
Firefighters work at a site of an apartment building hit by a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine September 11, 2026. REUTERS/Gleb Garanich

Sept 15 (Reuters) - A drone hit a petrol station in Ukraine's capital of Kyiv early on Tuesday, Mayor Vitali Klitschko ‌said on the Telegram messaging app, adding that there ‌was also a strike on warehouse facilities in another part of the city.

A Reuters ​witness heard an explosion in Kyiv.

The attack comes after U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to hit each other's energy targets.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Russia has recently started hitting petrol stations ‌in Kyiv, expanding the ⁠range of target facilities. In recent months, Russia hit some 300 petrol stations, mainly in or near ⁠Ukraine's frontline regions.

As Moscow was striking Ukraine, neighbouring Poland has commenced military aviation operations as a preventive measure to secure its airspace, Poland's ​Armed ​Forces said in a statement on ​social media website X.

In ‌Russia, which invaded Ukraine in 2022, a Ukraine missile attack has damaged a warehouse of the e-commerce company Ozon in the southern port city of Taganrog, among other facilities, regional governor said on Telegram.

Separately, a drone attack has hit an industrial facility in Samara ‌region on the Volga River, Governor ​Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said on Telegram, without naming ​it. The region is ​home to a number of large oil refineries.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Reuters could ‌not immediately independently verify the ​reports.

President Volodymyr Zelenskiy ​said on Monday that Kyiv was ready to support a U.S. proposal for a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire on energy sites only ​if Washington could ensure ‌Moscow was genuinely ready to end its war on ​Ukraine.

(Reporting by Gleb Garanich in Kyiv and Jekaterīna Golubkova ​in Tokyo; Editing by Tom Hogue)
